title: Weighing What Cannot Be Seen
paragraphs: No one has ever seen dark matter. Its existence is inferred, and the inference deserves scrutiny because it rests on an assumption that usually goes unstated: that the gravity we understand from the solar system behaves the same way across entire galaxies.

The first hints came in the nineteen thirties, when Fritz Zwicky studied the Coma cluster and found its galaxies moving too fast to be held together by the visible mass alone. In the nineteen seventies, Vera Rubin and her colleagues measured how quickly stars orbit in spiral galaxies. Stars far from the centre moved roughly as fast as those nearer in, whereas the visible matter implied they should slow down, much as the outer planets circle the Sun more slowly than the inner ones.

Faced with such a mismatch, physicists had two broad options. They could add mass that does not shine, keeping the familiar law intact, or they could revise the law and make do with the mass they could see. Most chose the first path, and the unseen mass became dark matter. A minority, following Mordehai Milgrom's proposal of modified Newtonian dynamics, chose the second.

What persuades most astronomers is not any single observation but convergence. In the Bullet Cluster, where two clusters of galaxies collided, gravitational lensing places most of the mass apart from the hot gas that holds most of the ordinary matter. Each line of evidence might be explained differently; together they are far harder to dismiss.

Still, the case remains circumstantial in a precise sense. Laboratory searches for the particles proposed as dark matter have not yet produced a confirmed detection, so the substance is known by its effects on what we can see. That is no scandal; much of science has worked this way. It is, however, a reason to hold the conclusion firmly and any particular account of it more loosely.

sources.claim: Fritz Zwicky 1930'larda Coma kümesindeki gökadaların görünür kütleyle bir arada tutulamayacak kadar hızlı hareket ettiğini buldu.
Vera Rubin ve meslektaşları 1970'lerde sarmal gökadalarda merkezden uzak yıldızların beklenenden hızlı (yaklaşık sabit hızla) dolandığını ölçtü.
Mermi Kümesi'nde kütle çekimsel merceklenme kütlenin çoğunu, sıradan maddenin çoğunu barındıran sıcak gazdan ayrı konumlandırır.
